blocks.note: surface reading: a gentle curse word, the kind said when something goes slightly wrong
setter's reading: the same, taken straight; in 1930 many clues were plain definitions

explanation.walkthrough: This early Times clue has no wordplay: it is a straight definition, and the crossing letters do the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Said as an exclamation of annoyance, the word is a polite stand-in for stronger swearing.

blocks.note: surface reading: an awkward or tricky label to give someone
setter's reading: the title, split after its second letter, reads as an instruction to turn into glue

explanation.walkthrough: A begum is a title for a Muslim woman of high rank in South Asia; split it and it reads 'be gum', which is sticky.
explanation.definitionFit: Begum is an honorific given to a Muslim princess or lady of rank, so it is a title or designation.

blocks.note: surface reading: something came after the older generation, or pursued them
setter's reading: the long trailing part of an old-fashioned skirt literally followed behind its wearer

explanation.surface: A fashion or habit that succeeded our grandmothers' day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Followed' means trailed along behind on the floor, not came later.
explanation.definitionFit: A train is the trailing back portion of a long gown, common in Victorian dress.

blocks.note: surface reading: an instruction printed in a play script
setter's reading: the same, one of the commonest such instructions

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition by example: scripts say 'Enter Hamlet' when an actor comes on.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the standard script instruction telling an actor to come on stage.

clue.text: It was not exactly child's play to make this.

definitions.text: It was not exactly child's play to make this

blocks.clueFragment: It was not exactly child's play to make this
blocks.note: surface reading: making this was harder than it looks
setter's reading: children, usually girls, did make these as needlework practice, but it was laborious work rather than play

explanation.walkthrough: 'Child's play' means something easy, but the joke is that children really did stitch these.
explanation.definitionFit: A sampler is an embroidered panel of alphabets and stitches, traditionally worked by young girls to show their skill.

clue.text: There may be a dangerous bird in this bush.

definitions.text: There may be a dangerous bird in this bush

blocks.clueFragment: There may be a dangerous bird in this bush
blocks.note: surface reading: a shrub that might hide some fierce bird
setter's reading: bird is slang for a person, so a dangerous fellow lies hidden waiting to attack, and the word itself ends in bush

explanation.surface: A walker is warned that a fierce bird may be lurking in a particular shrub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' as slang for a person turns the nature scene into an attacker lying in wait; the answer conveniently contains the word bush.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden attacker waiting to spring a surprise attack is lying in this, often in undergrowth.

blocks.note: surface reading: an exception, not applying to the present matter
setter's reading: this clue is a down entry, so the other crossword direction does not apply to it

explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to itself: it sits in the Down list, so the answer is the direction it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword entries run either down or in the other direction, and this down entry is not the horizontal kind.

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone announces they will call out a state, as in a geography quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal here: the solver must notice that the first two words contain the answer's letters rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is the north-easternmost state of the USA.

indicators.note: one thing placed after another comes next in line, so the words are joined with the second first

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thought about the generation that will follow ours.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is wordplay: put age after us. The answer is otherwise undefined, as in some early puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue gives no separate meaning; the word built means customary practice or the way something is used.

blocks.note: to aspirate is to sound an h, so the letter is breathed on
an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A phonetics note about a border pronounced with a breathy start.
explanation.walkthrough: Put an h-sound before EDGE; and the result is itself a border, a row of shrubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedge is a line of bushes forming the boundary of a garden or field.

clue.text: A rat will make game of this.

definitions.text: A rat will make game of this

blocks.clueFragment: A rat will make game of this
blocks.note: surface reading: a rodent mocking or teasing something
setter's reading: add the letters of rat to the answer and you get the name of a card game

explanation.surface: A cheeky rodent pokes fun at something.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'make game of' is to mock, but here it means 'turn into a game': the answer plus RAT gives BACCARAT, the casino card game. BACCA is a botanical word for a berry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacca is the Latin-derived botanical term for a berry, and with three more letters it becomes the card game baccarat.

clue.text: This god seems to have been exasperatingly deaf.

blocks.clueFragment: This god seems to have been exasperatingly deaf
blocks.note: surface reading: a deity who would not hear prayers
setter's reading: in the Bible his prophets cried to him all day with no answer, while Elijah mocked them

explanation.surface: A complaint about a deity who never seems to answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 Kings 18: the prophets of this Canaanite god called on him from morning to noon, 'but there was no voice, nor any that answered'.
explanation.definitionFit: Baal was the Canaanite deity whose prophets competed with Elijah on Mount Carmel.

blocks.note: surface reading: a town in the English county of Lincolnshire
setter's reading: the same, a plain general-knowledge definition

explanation.walkthrough: A plain general-knowledge clue; Lincolnshire is a county on England's east coast, and the crossing letters narrow the choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Grantham is a market town in south Lincolnshire, on the old Great North Road.

blocks.note: surface reading: the colour blue marks someone out, like a sporting Blue at Oxford or Cambridge
setter's reading: the answer follows blue to name the highest honour, as in the transatlantic liners' prize

explanation.surface: Being awarded a blue is a mark of honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'blue riband' is the top prize, originally the blue ribbon of the Garter and later the record for the fastest Atlantic crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: Riband is an old spelling of ribbon, and the blue riband stands for the highest honour in a field.

blocks.note: surface reading: the earliest item of clothing anyone wore
setter's reading: in Genesis, Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together to make these, the first clothes in the Bible

explanation.walkthrough: Genesis 3:7 in the King James Bible: they 'sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible's first mention of clothing is fig-leaf aprons, so this is the original garment.

clue.text: This baboon looks like a man at exercise.

blocks.note: taken as written
drill is military exercise, marching and so on

explanation.surface: A zoo visitor remarks that a baboon resembles a soldier doing his exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise' here is the soldier's kind, square-bashing on the parade ground, not a gym workout.
explanation.definitionFit: The mandrill is a large West African primate of the baboon family, famous for its red and blue face.

blocks.note: surface reading: a flower that grows in, or is blown by, the wind
setter's reading: the plant's common name, a translation of its Greek name

explanation.walkthrough: The Greek name comes from anemos, wind, and windflower is its English common name.
explanation.definitionFit: Windflower is the traditional English name for this buttercup-family plant.

blocks.note: surface reading: the units of a chain of flowers, or shops in a florist chain
setter's reading: the flowers children thread together stem to stem

explanation.walkthrough: A daisy chain is made by slitting each stem and threading the next flower through.
explanation.definitionFit: Children make garlands by linking these small white flowers together by their stems.

blocks.note: surface reading: a bugbear that troubled Julius Caesar in the month of March
setter's reading: the day he was warned of, and on which he was murdered

explanation.walkthrough: A soothsayer told Caesar 'Beware the Ides of March', the 15th, the day of his assassination in 44 BC.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the ides fell on the 15th of March, the date Caesar dreaded.

blocks.note: surface reading: the left wings of birds or buildings tend to do something
setter's reading: left-wing factions of political parties are prone to breaking away

explanation.surface: An observation that left wings have a certain habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left wings' is the political sense: radical factions that split off from their parties.
explanation.definitionFit: To secede is to withdraw formally from a party or union, something breakaway factions habitually do.

blocks.note: surface reading: an upbeat or confident faith
setter's reading: Positivism, the philosophy whose founder also launched a Religion of Humanity

explanation.walkthrough: Auguste Comte founded Positivism and its secular 'Religion of Humanity'; his system is named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Comtism is the positivist philosophy of Auguste Comte, which he turned into a humanist church.

blocks.note: surface reading: the tax payable on goods at the customs office
setter's reading: what you are obliged to do there, namely state the goods you carry

explanation.walkthrough: 'Duty' looks like the customs tax, but it means obligation: travellers must list dutiable goods.
explanation.definitionFit: At customs, travellers are required to state any taxable goods they are carrying.

blocks.note: surface reading: a length just short of four inches
setter's reading: the metric unit closest to that length

explanation.walkthrough: The clue asks for a metric unit: ten centimetres is about 3.94 inches.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenth of a metre measures 3.94 inches, so it falls just short of four.

blocks.note: surface reading: the dull look on a cow-like face
setter's reading: what a cow says

explanation.walkthrough: 'Expression' is the sound a cow utters, not a facial look.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lowing call of cattle, written as a word.

blocks.note: surface reading: a spinner of thread, a bowler, or a fishing lure
setter's reading: a child's toy that spins on its point

explanation.walkthrough: One of several things that spin; the toy fits the three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A top is a toy designed to rotate on a point when whipped or twisted.

clue.text: Ely was named after this, says Isaak Walton.

definitions.text: Ely was named after this, says Isaak Walton

blocks.clueFragment: Ely was named after this, says Isaak Walton
blocks.note: surface reading: a piece of place-name lore from the angler-author
setter's reading: the cathedral city's name is said to come from the fish once plentiful in the surrounding fens

explanation.surface: A literary aside on how a cathedral city got its name.
explanation.walkthrough: Ely is a cathedral city in the Cambridgeshire fens; Walton's 'The Compleat Angler' (1653) repeats the tradition that it was named for its abundant fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The fenland around Ely teemed with these snake-like fish, which were even used to pay rents.

blocks.note: surface reading: a gale or punch with a whiff of the sea about it
setter's reading: the word for a slap is also a word for a taste, and for a small fishing boat

explanation.surface: A sea wind, or a sailor's punch, tastes of the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does three jobs: a blow, a savour (as in 'smacks of'), and a single-masted fishing vessel, which supplies the nautical flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack is a sharp slap, a flavour or trace, and also a type of fishing boat.

blocks.note: surface reading: a law passed by the legislature
setter's reading: an action Parliament performs, meeting in session

explanation.walkthrough: 'Act of Parliament' normally means a statute; here it is something Parliament does.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament is said to sit when it is in session, conducting business.

blocks.note: surface reading
setter's reading: the little word written out twice forms a term meaning middling

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is literally the word so twice, and that doubled form means 'only fair'.
explanation.definitionFit: So-so means mediocre or indifferent, and is spelt as two copies of the same word.

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the word before it is read from its last letter back

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A familiar saying: the flow of the sea, or of fortune, has changed direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is wordplay: read tide the other way round. The setter leaves the answer undefined, which early puzzles sometimes did.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue gives no separate meaning; the answer is simply the word that the turned-round tide spells, meaning to revise text.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone glances about and then trips, or a joke that fails
setter's reading: an object that appears circular and lies flat when it drops

explanation.surface: A comedian glances about the room and the joke fails to land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks' means appears, not glances; 'falls flat' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is a thin, flat, circular object.

blocks.note: surface reading: anything connected with Shakespeare is worth a lot
setter's reading: the large-format early collected edition of the plays, a famously costly book

explanation.surface: A collector notes that anything Shakespearean commands a high price.
explanation.walkthrough: The First Folio of 1623 collected Shakespeare's plays; copies are among the most valuable printed books.
explanation.definitionFit: A folio is a large book made from sheets folded once, and Shakespeare's First Folio is a prized rarity.

clue.text: Starts to be polite but becomes just civil.

blocks.clueFragment: Starts to be polite but becomes just civil
blocks.note: surface reading: someone begins courteously but cools to mere civility
setter's reading: the word opens with the letters of polite, minus its last, and ends meaning civil in the sense of relating to the state

explanation.surface: A frosty encounter in which warmth fades to bare politeness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civil' looks like 'courteous' but is used in its public sense, as in civil or political rights; the word begins POLIT, almost polite.
explanation.definitionFit: Civil and political both describe matters of citizens and the state, as in civil liberties or political rights.

blocks.note: surface reading: a king or prince at the centre of an ancient Athenian play
setter's reading: the same, a straight definition

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge clue: Sophocles' 'Oedipus Rex' is the best-known Greek tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Oedipus, king of Thebes, is the protagonist of Sophocles' tragedies.

definitions.note: a noun, where the answer is the verb meaning to imprison

indicators.note: sounding like something means the words are compared by ear, not spelling

blocks.note: doing things by rotation is doing them one after another

explanation.surface: A prisoner's spell in custody that rotates among several people.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as: the word for imprisonment sounds like the phrase for 'by rotation'. The definition sits mid-clue, an early-puzzle freedom.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern is to confine someone, especially enemy nationals in wartime, without trial.

clue.text: A word in this is helpful.

explanation.walkthrough: 'A word in season' (Isaiah 50:4, Proverbs 15:23) is apt, well-timed advice.
explanation.definitionFit: In the phrase 'a word in season' the noun means the right or fitting time, which is what makes advice helpful.

clue.text: Generally something to be said on both.

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'there is something to be said on both sides' supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: In an argument the two opposing positions are its two sides.

blocks.note: surface reading: a thorough test or inspection

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition of the accountant's scrutiny of the books.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is an official, detailed inspection of financial records.

blocks.note: surface reading: the last glowing coal in a dying fire

blocks.note: surface reading: a romance carried on by someone banished abroad

explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of desire, and the popular name for the Piccadilly statue.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone whose attempts at comfort only make things worse

explanation.definitionFit: Elihu, son of Barachel, rebukes Job in chapters 32 to 37 of the biblical book.

clue.text: House agents' name for the exiguous.

clue.text: Model of vigilance made out of sugar.

blocks.note: surface reading: a king of some prosperous era

explanation.walkthrough: A general-knowledge clue from Roman myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman legend held that the god Saturn reigned over Italy during a mythical era of peace and abundance.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who was a companion of the novelist

explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's last finished novel is 'Our Mutual Friend' (1865); the answer is the word describing that friend.
